'''Macaulay brackets''' are a notation used to describe the [[ramp function]]

:<math>\{x\} = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ x, & x \ge 0. \end{cases}</math>

A popular alternative transcription uses angle brackets, ''viz.'' <math>\langle x \rangle</math>.<ref>[http://www.colorado.edu/engineering/CAS/courses.d/Structures.d/IAST.Lect12.d/IAST.Lect12.pdf Lecture 12: Beam Deflections by Discontinuity Functions.] Introduction to Aerospace Structures. Department of Aerospace Engineering Sciences, University of Colorado at Boulder </ref> 
Another commonly used notation is <math>x</math><sub>+</sub> or <math>(x)</math><sub>+</sub> for the [[positive number|positive]] part of <math>x</math>, which avoids conflicts with <math>\{...\}</math> for [[set notation]].

== In engineering ==
Macaulay's notation is commonly used in the static analysis of bending moments of a beam. This is useful because shear forces applied on a member render the [[shear and moment diagram]] discontinuous. Macaulay's notation also provides an easy way of integrating these discontinuous curves to give bending moments, angular deflection, and so on. For engineering purposes, angle brackets are often used to denote the use of [[Macaulay's method]].

:<math>\langle x-a\rangle^n = \begin{cases} 0, & x < a \\ (x-a)^n, & x \ge a. \end{cases}</math> <math> (n \ge 0)</math>

The above example simply states that the function takes the value <math>(x-a)^n</math> for all ''x'' values larger than ''a''. With this, all the forces acting on a beam can be added, with their respective points of action being the value of ''a''.

A particular case is the [[unit step function]],
:<math>\langle x-a\rangle^0 \equiv \{x-a\}^0 = \begin{cases} 0, & x < a \\ 1, & x \ge a. \end{cases}</math>
